question: arXiv:2209.00006v2 compares the best-fit spectra of its Galactic Center excess candidates when each is fitted together with ring-based templates. Which candidate gives the faintest excess, and how good is its fit? What does the paper say about the spectra of the candidates that include the boxy bulge? And how does the dark matter spectrum obtained with the ring-based templates compare with those spectra and with the dark matter result obtained with the astrophysics-based templates of Cholis et al.?

arguments.answer:
The faintest excess with the ring-based templates is the X-shaped bulge, which is also the worst fit. Its −2ΔlnL is +30 relative to no excess, so it fits slightly worse than having no excess at all. Its Δln B is −190.

Every excess that includes the boxy bulge has a very similar spectrum. This covers the boxy bulge alone, the boxy bulge plus the nuclear stellar bulge, and the boxy bulge together with the X-shaped bulge. The paper calls these spectra relatively soft, and says they are compatible with having absorbed unmodeled diffuse flux.

The dark matter spectrum from the ring-based fit is harder on average than the boxy-bulge spectra. It is similar in shape to the dark matter spectrum from the Cholis et al. astrophysics-based templates, but lower in flux. It also shows "wiggles" between energy bins that neither dark matter annihilation nor millisecond pulsars predict.
